newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria steps up fight against video, audio piracy.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria steps up fight against video, audio piracy.

text.p: Bulgaria is stepping up controls on audio and video piracy in response to Western criticism, a government official said on Wednesday.
Washington put Bulgaria on a "watch list" in October which will increase pressure on the country to improve protection of intellectual property rights, officials said.

"We have prepared a document to be presented to the government for the establishment of a commission on copyright control which involves seven ministries, police and legal authorities," said Dimitar Enchev, director of the culture ministry's National Centre for Copyright Protection (NCCP).

In April the government adopted a final document which requires all manufacturers of sound recordings to verify the orders they receive with the NCCP and thus make sure they are legitimate, Enchev told a news conference.
Since November an identification code engraved on compact discs to identify the producer has been introduced in Bulgaria and now five companies are using it.
"Bulgaria is the only country in Central and Eastern Europe which has introduced the identification code," Enchev said.
In the first eight months of 1996, Bulgarian customs seized almost 24,000 illegal CDs at border points which were intended for export, Enchev said.

"Most of the illegal production is exported to the former Soviet republics," Enchev said, adding that the capacity of the CD production lines in Bulgaria was much greater than the needs of the Bulgarian music market.
In the same period police investigated more than 200 audio and video producers and distributors and 83 cases were referred to the prosecutor's office, he said.
The NCCP confiscated more than 23,000 audio and video cassettes between January and September, Enchev said.
The first court case in Bulgaria for copyright abuse was on September 23 against the owner of a cable television network who was given a two-year suspended sentence and fined 200,000 levs ($412,400).

Earlier this year major music companies expressed concern about delay in copyright law enforcement in Bulgaria saying it was preventing them from investing there. Intellectual property theft has been illegal since June 1995.
Officials have said counterfeit music cassettes, compact discs and videotapes made up some 87 percent of the local market in 1994 and some 80 percent in 1995.
Bulgaria has joined the Rome and Geneva conventions, which set the standards for protecting intellectual property.
